The book’s central argument

The Revelation

In Enchantress Athena, Johnson argues that Greek religious thought and philosophy shaped later Christian doctrine. He centers his inquiry on what he calls a three-part spell—the riddle, the taboo, and the threat—and traces its echoes through the Athanasian Creed and the history of Christendom.

The author’s theological interpretation

Three ideas at the heart of the book

The Ancient Spell

Johnson connects three symbols on Athena’s Parthenon image with the riddle, taboo, and threat he identifies in the creed. These are the book’s interpretations of those symbols.

01

The Riddle

The sphinx on Athena’s helmet is presented in the book as a symbol of riddles.

02

The Taboo

Johnson reads the Gorgon Medusa on the breastplate as a warning against questioning.

03

The Threat

The serpent on Athena’s shield is linked to the creed’s warnings of punishment.

Inside the book

Enchantress Athena

Her Ancient Spell on Modern Christendom presents Johnson’s argument about Athena’s influence on Christian doctrine. The chapters examine Greek philosophy, Paul’s teaching, the Council of Nikea, Augustine, Aquinas, Dante, and images of Athena around the world. The book’s claims are presented here as the author’s theological reading.

Chapter 1

Introduces the central thesis and the book’s framing of the “spell.”

Chapter 2

Explores the connection Johnson draws between Athena and the Genesis serpent.

Chapter 6 · 325 AD

Emperor Constantine and the Council of Nikea

Examines the council and its place in the author’s account.

Chapters 9–13

Greek Myths, Medieval Writers, and Images

Topics include eternal torment, Aquinas, Dante, Gothic cathedrals, and tapestries.
